J.B. Hunt Transport is urging the Surface Transportation Board to reject Union Pacific’s (NYSE: UNP ) proposed merger with Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ), arguing that the deal overstates potential shipper savings and truck-to-rail growth while threatening competition and service reliability.
In comments filed Nov. 18, the transportation company (NASDAQ: JBHT ) said the merger, as proposed, would likely deliver “more harm than benefit” to its intermodal customers. It argued that the railroads have not provided adequate assurances that operating efficiencies would translate into lower customer costs or that intermodal shippers would have meaningful remedies for service failures.
The filing signed by Darren Field, Hunt’s executive vice president and president of intermodal, said that the company moved approximately 2.25 million intermodal loads in the preceding 12 months and is the largest intermodal customer of both BNSF Railway (NYSE: BRK-B ) as part of the railroad’s Quantum service, and Norfolk Southern. It also has commercial relationships with every Class I railroad.
Hunt took particular issue with the railroads’ projection that the merger would generate approximately 1.2 million annual intermodal loads converted from highway transportation, phased in over three years. The company argued that the forecast does not reflect how customers actually choose between truck and rail service.
According to the filing, the railroads’ model uses haul length and interchange information as a proxy for reliability. Hunt said that approach overlooks other causes of service failures, including freight left behind at origin terminals, congestion, equipment shortages and delays at destinations.
“But moving the dots on a map to create different single-line origins and destinations does not, by itself, give a customer a reason to move freight from highway to intermodal,” Field said in the filing.
Field contrasted the projected growth with Hunt’s own experience. The company’s largest intermodal growth year, 2013, added 181,000 loads, he said. In 2016, a strategy using steep price discounts generated 144,000 additional loads, below a target of 200,000. Those results illustrate the challenge of achieving the railroads’ conversion forecast, he argued.
Hunt said substantial conversion opportunities already exist without consolidation. Its internal research estimates that approximately 9.8 million to 11.2 million annual loads could shift from truck to intermodal across all Class I railroads using existing routes and arrangements between carriers.
Savings claims leave cost questions
The company also challenged the railroads’ projected $3.5 billion in annual shipper savings, arguing that the application does not guarantee that merger efficiencies would reach customers through lower rates. It warned that rate increases could instead absorb some or all of the projected difference between truck and rail costs.
The filing said the cost estimates understate the expense of converting freight to intermodal, including first- and last-mile trucking, containers, chassis and terminal capacity. Field estimated that handling an additional 1.2 million annual intermodal loads would require more than 60,000 additional 53-foot containers, along with supporting equipment and capacity.
Hunt said the application does not explain who would supply that equipment, who would pay for it or how quickly it could be integrated into the network. Failure to secure sufficient capacity could undermine reliability and push freight back onto highways, the company argued.
Harrisburg routing options raise concerns
Competition concerns center partly on the possibility that a combined Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern would favor freight moving entirely over its own network over traffic exchanged with competing railroads. Hunt identified BNSF–Norfolk Southern service into Eastern Pennsylvania as a particular concern.
The company described Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, as a network-critical intermodal market and a significant opportunity for future growth. Today, freight can reach that market from either Union Pacific or BNSF through interchange with Norfolk Southern in Chicago, according to the filing. Hunt warned that the merger could weaken BNSF’s participation and reduce customers’ competitive routing alternatives.
To illustrate its concerns about gateway protections, the provider cited its experience following the Canadian Pacific (NYSE: CP )–Kansas City Southern merger. The company said unreliable service and rate increases led it to stop using the Laredo, Texas, gateway for its traffic despite protections adopted in that proceeding.
Field said an alternative Monterrey, Mexico-to-Atlanta route using Ferromex, BNSF and Norfolk Southern through Eagle Pass and Chicago was 1,570 rail miles longer than the CPKC–Norfolk Southern route through Laredo, yet moved freight faster and more consistently. Hunt argued that the experience shows why keeping an interchange formally open is not enough to preserve a commercially viable option.
Conditions sought if merger is approved
Although rejection is its preferred outcome, J.B. Hunt outlined four categories of protections it wants imposed if the STB approves the transaction:
Preserve existing gateways, interchanges and service lanes, with prior STB approval required before they are eliminated, downgraded, restricted or otherwise disadvantaged;
Grant competing railroads trackage rights into Harrisburg—BNSF from Chicago, CSX (NASDAQ: CSX ) from Chambersburg, Pennsylvania, or both;
Establish enforceable intermodal service standards, accessible dispute-resolution procedures and financial penalties or damages for noncompliance;
Require rigorous STB oversight for at least 10 years.
Hunt also argued that the proposed service protections leave intermodal customers without adequate recourse. Its filing said intermodal traffic is excluded from the railroads’ proposed damages arbitration and Targeted Access programs, and that those programs would remain too restrictive even if eligibility were expanded.
Why It Matters: J.B. Hunt’s filing challenges the merger from the perspective of a major customer of both Norfolk Southern and its competitors, and not simply a rival railroad. Its central argument is that a larger network does not automatically produce a better door-to-door transportation service: customers also need competitive prices, dependable equipment and capacity, reliable delivery and viable alternative routes.

Mercedes-Benz's New Electric Two-Seater Chassis Mule Sure Looks Weird, Is the SLC Coming Back?
14 photos
Photo: Baldauf
Could Mercedes be working on an electric roadster here, probably an electric take on the SLC as an alternative to the Porsche 718 Boxster in full-electric specification? We don't know for certain, but from the looks of it, a two-seater chassis test mule with a rear-mounted electric drive unit suggests exactly that.
There is no bodywork to speak of, no doors, and no windshield either. Barely anything resembles a cabin at this point, and the amount of plywood used to make this mule happen beggars belief. Built around a black-painted frame, the vehicle also shows exposed suspension componentry and a rear-mounted battery.
Said high-voltage pack is relatively small and is located right behind the rear motor. It literally hangs out beyond the rear axle, which is the kind of location that made me remember the Ford Pinto scandal from the 1970s. The TL;DR version is a fuel tank design flaw that made the American subcompact prone to catching fire in rear-end collisions.
The battery's location is all the more weird once you remember that Porsche went in a completely different direction with the zero-emission 718 range . Instead of packaging the high-voltage pack underfloor, as you'd expect from a conventional electric vehicle, the E-Core layout mounts the battery behind the rear seats, mimicking a mid-engine configuration.
Stacking it vertically behind the rear seats definitely helps with weight distribution, but this layout also enables a low seating position and reproduces the polar moment of inertia of a mid-engine sports car. Porsche's battery uses three modules stacked across two vertical levels, and curiously enough, it rocks prismatic cells instead of cylindrical cells.
Photo: Baldauf Accommodating two people, the Mercedes test mule is pictured with a laptop in the passenger's lap. Definitely a work in progress, the open-top mule features pretty substantial rear control arms and unusually high front suspension mounts. We can further see how the steering column sits unusually far back, indicating a very long hood for whatever production model may transpire from this fellow.
All of these elements, combined with the relatively short wheelbase, made us wonder if an electric SL or SLC is under development. The SLC route seems the most plausible, and there is some historical context to back the roadster hunch up.
Back in 2021, then development chief Markus Schaefer confirmed that AMG was considering an electric ragtop . Schaefer stepped down as CTO last year, leaving the company in December 2025. While Schaefer acknowledged that the business case was difficult to make due to declining demand for such vehicles, he nevertheless considered the open-top electric AMG an appealing proposition.
The automaker's electric vehicle strategy has shifted dramatically since 2021, with Mercedes favoring combustion and hybrid alternatives alongside electric models nowadays. Mercedes hasn't confirmed the existence of this odd platform or named a future application for it, making the e-roadster mule all the more mysterious.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) on Nov. 9 issued its first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) in nearly six decades, authorizing construction of four X-energy Xe-100 reactors that could supply electricity and high-temperature process steam to Dow’s chemical manufacturing operations on the Texas Gulf Coast. While the authorization follows nearly eight years of technical and regulatory engagement between X-energy and the NRC, development of the first commercial Xe-100 facility will require extensive engineering, fuel and materials qualification, component procurement and manufacturing, and a series of capital investment decisions by Dow.
The construction permit (CPAR-3) , issued to Long Mott Energy LLC, a wholly owned Dow subsidiary, authorizes construction of the proposed Long Mott Generating Station in Calhoun County, Texas. The facility is expected to comprise four helium-cooled, graphite-moderated pebble-bed reactors, each rated at 200 MW of thermal capacity (MWth) and 80 MW of electrical capacity (MWe), to replace aging energy and steam generation assets at Dow’s adjacent Seadrift Operations complex.
The NRC’s 852-page final safety evaluation report (FSER) , issued Oct. 30, and an independent assessment by its Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) detail the technical basis for construction authorization, the safety questions that remain to be resolved, and the extent of design and analytical work required before the facility can be licensed to operate. The regulatory record also sheds new light on Dow’s financial arrangements and its selection of a NextEra Energy Resources subsidiary to operate the plant.
The Long Mott authorization is the NRC’s third advanced reactor construction permit this year, following permits issued for TerraPower’s sodium-cooled Kemmerer Unit 1 in Wyoming on March 9 and the Tennessee Valley Authority’s (TVA’s) BWRX-300 light-water reactor at Clinch River in Tennessee on Sept. 28. As the NRC noted, the Long Mott permit marks several regulatory firsts for the agency: authorization of a multimodule advanced reactor facility, a pebble-bed reactor core, and a reactor design that refuels during operation, as well as the first HTGR review under the risk-informed Licensing Modernization Project framework.
Supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP), Long Mott is advancing through Dow’s phased capital investment process. According to X-energy, Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027, ahead of a separate final investment decision that would authorize full-scale nuclear construction. For now, the companies are targeting initial energy delivery in the early 2030s.
Eight Years of Regulatory Groundwork
The historic construction permit is the first for an HTGR since September 1968, when U.S. nuclear regulators authorized Public Service Co. of Colorado to build Fort St. Vrain, an 842-MWth plant that used prismatic graphite fuel blocks and subsequently supplied electricity to the Colorado grid. While Long Mott would have nearly the same thermal capacity—800 MWth—it would distribute heat production across four continuously refueled pebble-bed reactors designed to supply both electricity and industrial process steam.
X-energy began pre-application engagement with the NRC in 2018, two years before the DOE selected the Xe-100 for one of its two principal ARDP demonstration awards. At the time, the company envisioned deploying its first four-reactor facility with Energy Northwest in Washington state by 2028. The demonstration, however, took a markedly different direction in March 2023, when X-energy signed a joint development agreement with Dow and shifted the project to the Texas Gulf Coast . The DOE added Dow as a sub-awardee under the ARDP cooperative agreement, and the companies committed to an engineering program valued at up to $50 million, including preparation of a construction permit application. The change introduced an industrial application for the first commercial demonstration of the Xe-100, though the DOE retained Energy Northwest as a sub-awardee to preserve the potential for a subsequent Washington deployment.
Dow and X-energy selected Seadrift in May 2023 . By the time Long Mott Energy submitted its construction permit application on March 31, 2025 , several of the analytical methodologies needed to establish the Xe-100’s safety basis had already undergone individual NRC reviews. X-energy says it has now secured approval of 14 topical reports that apply generically to the Xe-100, covering some of the most technically demanding aspects of licensing a gas-cooled pebble-bed reactor: fuel and graphite qualification, reactor core behavior, thermal-hydraulic transients, radioactive material releases and atmospheric dispersion, emergency planning, and control room staffing. Developers of subsequent Xe-100 projects can incorporate those methodologies by reference, subject to their prescribed limitations and conditions, though each facility will require an individual licensing review.
Integral to Long Mott’s application was the Licensing Modernization Project (LMP) methodology, an industry-developed approach to licensing non-light-water reactors that the NRC endorsed in 2020 through Regulatory Guide 1.233 . The methodology, notably, uses the frequency and radiological consequences of postulated events to inform which safety functions a reactor must perform, which equipment it relies on to perform them, and whether the design incorporates adequate defense-in-depth.
For the Xe-100, the five fundamental safety functions are retaining radionuclides, controlling reactivity, controlling heat removal, controlling water and steam ingress, and maintaining geometry. The resulting classification of structures, systems, and components as safety-related, non-safety-related with special treatment, or non-safety-related without special treatment has implications well beyond the safety analysis itself. It informs how equipment will be specified, procured, qualified, and maintained throughout the plant’s operating life.
The NRC accepted Long Mott Energy’s application for docketing on May 12, 2025, and established an 18-month review schedule the following month. In May 2026, as POWER reported , the NRC issued its final environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact, determining that the project did not warrant preparation of an environmental impact statement (EIS).
By September, Long Mott Energy had incorporated eight supplements into a consolidated revision of its application, six addressing the preliminary safety analysis report and two concerning general and financial information and regulatory exemptions. The NRC held its mandatory hearing on Sept. 22. The ACRS reported to the Commission on Oct. 16 that its review “supports issuance of the construction permit,” and NRC staff completed the FSER later that month, one month ahead of its scheduled November milestone.
“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” NRC Chairman Ho Nieh said in the agency’s Nov. 9 announcement .
For X-energy, the licensing process has unfolded alongside a substantial overhaul of U.S. nuclear regulation. Congress, through the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act (NEIMA) of 2019 and the bipartisan Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy (ADVANCE) Act of 2024, directed the NRC to modernize its advanced reactor licensing framework, improve the predictability of reviews, and establish expedited licensing procedures. The reform effort intensified on May 23, 2025—just 11 days after the NRC accepted Long Mott’s application for docketing—when President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14300 , directing the agency to establish fixed licensing deadlines and undertake a comprehensive revision of its regulations and guidance. The NRC, notably, identified Long Mott’s 18-month review schedule among its initiatives to accelerate licensing .
“Getting the construction permit earlier than expected is reflective of the thorough and efficient work of the NRC, the reforms that have been put in place by the Congress over the last six years, and the phenomenal work of the X-energy and Dow teams,” X-energy CEO Clay Sell said in the companies’ joint announcement .
Engineering a Four-Reactor Industrial Nuclear Facility
Dow’s plans for the Xe-100 at Seadrift, where the company manufactures polyethylene, glycols, and oxide derivatives, hinge on the reactor’s ability to supply both electricity and high-temperature process steam. According to X-energy, the reactor can produce steam at temperatures of up to 565C (1,049F), considerably higher than those typically achieved by conventional light-water reactors, which could broaden the range of industrial applications for nuclear heat.
While Long Mott’s aggregate reactor capacity of 800 MWth corresponds to a nominal electrical generating capacity of 320 MWe, the plant’s proposed conventional island would incorporate turbine-generators, extraction steam systems, and dedicated process steam supply equipment to accommodate Seadrift’s electrical and thermal energy requirements. According to the FSER, any excess power would be exported to the electrical grid.
The Xe-100’s pebble-bed fuel configuration allows the reactor to be refueled during operation, an important consideration for industrial facilities that require a continuous supply of process steam. According to the FSER, each reactor core contains approximately 220,000 spherical fuel elements embedded with uranium oxycarbide tristructural isotropic (TRISO) coated fuel particles. Essentially, helium circulates through the pebble bed, transferring heat generated by fission to secondary-side water in the steam generator to produce superheated steam.
The fuel pebbles, meanwhile, circulate through a dedicated fuel handling system, which loads them at the top of the reactor vessel and conveys them using gravitational and pneumatic forces. The system measures the accumulated burnup of pebbles discharged from the bottom of the core and determines whether they should be returned to the reactor or transferred to storage. Operators can thus replenish the core continuously during operation, eliminating the need for the periodic batch refueling outages characteristic of conventional light-water reactors.
Although Long Mott would comprise four reactors, each rated at 200 MWth and equipped with its own steam generator, the NRC evaluated the facility as a single multimodule nuclear power plant. The four reactor and steam generator pairs would occupy a common nuclear island and share a reactor building foundation, a shield structure, and several auxiliary systems. The regulatory review, notably, assessed the safety implications of equipment sharing under the design’s Principal Design Criterion 5, which governs shared structures, systems, and components.
The proposed facility would occupy approximately 1,537 acres of Dow-owned land in the coastal prairie of the Guadalupe River delta, about 22 miles southeast of Victoria. Its proximity to an established petrochemical manufacturing complex required the NRC to evaluate potential hazards associated with industrial accidents, fires, toxic chemical releases, and the transportation of hazardous materials, in addition to the hurricanes and flooding characteristic of the Texas Gulf Coast.
Fuel Performance, Safety Analysis, and Design Qualification
Unlike conventional light-water reactors, the Xe-100 does not rely on a leak-tight, pressure-retaining containment structure. Instead, it incorporates what the NRC calls “functional containment”—a series of barriers to radioactive material transport, principally the successive coating layers surrounding individual TRISO fuel kernels. A central question in the NRC’s safety analysis was how well those coatings would retain fission products under prolonged neutron irradiation and at the elevated temperatures predicted under postulated accident conditions.
Fuel Performance and Accident Analysis. For a depressurized loss-of-forced-cooling event, Long Mott Energy calculated a nominal peak fuel temperature of 1,803C (3,277F), compared with 1,788C (3,250F) in the NRC’s independent confirmatory calculations using its MELCOR accident analysis code. The applicant’s calculated peak, however, rose to 1,885C (3,425F) when it incorporated analytical uncertainties.
The preliminary peak temperatures for the limiting design-basis accident, the NRC noted in its FSER, “are beyond the limits typically associated with TRISO fuel particles, including the results from the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Gas Reactor (AGR) program.” While the preliminary radiological analyses account for increased fission product releases at elevated temperatures and indicate a maximum 30-day dose of 14.4 rem at the exclusion area boundary—below the applicable 25-rem regulatory criterion—Long Mott Energy must further substantiate its fuel performance assumptions.
The ACRS, which supported issuance of the construction permit in its Oct. 16 letter to the Commission , similarly cautioned that “both fuel and structural materials are challenged by the peak temperatures predicted under limiting accident conditions.” The committee identified fuel performance, functional containment, mechanistic source term analysis—the assessment of radioactive material release and transport during an accident—and graphite and metallic component performance as areas that “require significant additional development.”
Notably, the committee questioned the use of correlations derived from uranium dioxide fuel in the applicant’s source term analysis, given that the Xe-100 uses uranium oxycarbide. It noted, however, that data from the AGR program show substantially lower cesium release from uranium oxycarbide and that the calculated doses are therefore likely conservative.
Long Mott Energy, meanwhile, has proposed a plume exposure pathway emergency planning zone extending 400 meters (about a quarter mile), compared with the roughly 10-mile zone generally associated with conventional U.S. light-water power reactors. The proposal draws on an X-energy methodology the NRC approved in February 2026, subject to seven limitations and conditions, though the agency will evaluate final emergency planning arrangements during its operating license review.
Qualification of the Final Design. Under the two-step licensing process established in Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) Part 50, the NRC can authorize construction before an applicant resolves all outstanding safety questions, provided the applicant establishes a research and development (R&D) program reasonably designed to resolve them before completing construction. Long Mott Energy, notably, did not request Commission approval of any design feature under 10 CFR 50.35(b), and it must substantiate its final design through a separate operating license application.
The NRC found that Long Mott Energy’s R&D program, which covers TRISO fuel, the graphite core assembly, and safety-related metallic components, is reasonably designed to resolve the outstanding safety questions. The NRC’s approval of X-energy’s graphite core assembly qualification and design methodologies alone carries 25 conditions that Long Mott Energy plans to address through testing, development of analytical methodologies, or both before completing its operating license application.
Engineering for Gulf Coast Flooding. At Seadrift, hurricane-driven storm surge presents a separate engineering challenge. While Long Mott Energy proposes a finished site grade of 31 feet for the nuclear island area relative to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88), its calculations indicate a stillwater storm surge elevation of 36.38 feet, rising to 46.49 feet when wave runup is included.
Because the applicant had not submitted detailed designs for site grading and passive flood protection features, the NRC stipulated in Paragraph 3.D of the construction permit that Long Mott Energy must notify the agency when those designs are available for examination. The permit anticipates that notification will occur before the placement of safety-significant concrete for structure foundations. The designs should demonstrate that safety-related structures, systems, and components, along with non-safety-related components that must remain functional, are protected during and after the design-basis flood.
Fuel qualification, flooding, and financial qualifications also featured in a contested licensing proceeding brought by the San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper. On Nov. 6, three days before the NRC issued the construction permit, the Commission denied the organization’s petition for review of six licensing board decisions and orders , leaving in place the board’s termination of the contested proceeding.
Dow’s Investment Decision and Federal Cost-Sharing
While Dow and X-energy initially envisioned a 2026 construction start and project completion by the end of the decade , Dow now projects construction could begin later this decade, with startup in the early 2030s. The chemical manufacturer has stressed, however, that securing a construction permit does not constitute a commitment to build Long Mott.
“As we move forward, we will continue to evaluate the project through the lens of competitiveness, execution readiness, and capital affordability before any decision regarding construction is made,” Edward Stones, Dow’s business vice president for energy and climate, said in the company’s Nov. 9 announcement .
During X-energy’s Nov. 12 earnings call, CEO Clay Sell elaborated on Dow’s formal investment decision process, through which the chemical manufacturer assesses whether engineering has sufficiently advanced, whether cost targets are being met, and whether operations and maintenance (O&M) assumptions have been validated before investment decisions reach its board. X-energy is still developing manufacturing drawings and detailed construction plans, Sell noted, and while the company does not expect to complete the final reactor design before Dow’s anticipated 2027 preliminary investment decision, it intends to do so before construction begins.
Sell underscored the importance of completing detailed engineering before construction, given the industry’s history of cost overruns and schedule delays. “Now we also have to avoid other mistakes that have been made in our industry in the past, like starting construction before you have it completely designed,” he told analysts. Sell did not, however, specify the level of engineering completion or the class of cost estimate Dow would require to sanction the investment.
Construction Financing and Federal Reimbursements. Although the companies have not publicly disclosed an overall construction cost estimate for Long Mott, Dow has committed to providing financial support exceeding half of the projected construction cost, according to the FSER. Under a Feb. 23, 2026, financial support agreement, The Dow Chemical Company agreed to fund construction costs up to a specified amount unless it secures substitute financial assurance through a loan facility, a letter of credit, or both, with the NRC’s written consent. The arrangement, notably, allows Long Mott Energy to incur project expenditures before receiving federal cost-sharing reimbursements under the ARDP.
On that basis, the NRC determined that Long Mott Energy appears financially qualified to undertake construction. The agency granted an exemption from the construction permit financial qualification requirements in 10 CFR 50.33(f) and Appendix C to Part 50, applying instead the standard under 10 CFR 70.23(a)(5), under which an applicant must appear financially qualified to engage in the proposed activities.
X-energy, meanwhile, said on Nov. 9 that it had been informed of an intended increase in the total value of its ARDP award to $2.15 billion, encompassing both the Long Mott demonstration and its TRISO-X fuel fabrication facility in Tennessee. The DOE had previously indicated it could invest up to $1.23 billion over seven years in the reactor and fuel facility, though the agency did not address the increased award amount in its Nov. 13 announcement on the construction permit .
X-energy reported $66.3 million in revenue and grant income for the third quarter of 2026, including $51.5 million in services revenue, primarily from Xe-100 design work under the ARDP, and $14.8 million in grant income tied to the Dow demonstration. The company incurred $71.8 million in capital expenditures for construction projects, including its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility, and received $27.8 million in associated cash reimbursements from the DOE during the quarter.
X-energy Chief Financial Officer Daniel Gross told analysts that cumulative ARDP reimbursements had reached $618 million through September 2026. While the program reimburses roughly half of eligible expenditures, Gross noted that X-energy must first incur the costs and invoice the DOE, and its financial statements also include capital and operating expenditures from other projects that do not qualify for federal cost-sharing.
Operating License and Construction Schedule. Long Mott’s construction permit specifies July 1, 2033, as the earliest date for completion of construction and Dec. 31, 2033, as the latest. The permit expires on the latter date unless the NRC extends it. X-energy has already begun developing the operating license application, which Sell anticipates filing approximately two years before commissioning, allowing for an expected 18-month NRC review ahead of initial fuel loading and startup.
For subsequent Xe-100 deployments, X-energy expects to reuse much of the engineering and safety analysis undertaken for Long Mott, particularly for the standardized nuclear island, which comprises the reactor and nuclear steam supply system. Sell said the company anticipates substantially shorter construction permit reviews for subsequent applications, citing unofficial indications from the NRC that the agency is targeting review periods of six to 12 months.
Project Delivery and the Xe-100 Supply Chain
Still, while Dow is evaluating the investment, X-energy has committed its own capital to reserve manufacturing capacity and procure long-lead materials, including graphite, steel forgings, and steam generator tubing. “We’ve chosen to make some early investments to secure capacity and to buy early material with the full expectation that when our customers reach their investment decisions, they will take over those obligations on a go-forward basis,” Sell told analysts.
Project Engineering and Nuclear Operations. Dow, notably, has enlisted NextEra Energy Resources to provide technical support in nuclear procurement, licensing, personnel training, and the development of operating disciplines. According to the FSER, Long Mott Energy has also selected a subsidiary of NextEra Energy Resources to operate the facility. In assessing Long Mott Energy’s technical qualifications, the NRC considered the complementary expertise of the three companies: Dow’s experience in industrial energy production and large capital projects, X-energy’s reactor engineering capabilities, and the operating experience of NextEra Energy’s nuclear fleet, which comprises seven light-water reactors across four sites.
Fluor, a U.S. engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) firm, has also secured engineering contracts for X-energy’s two most advanced U.S. reactor projects. On Nov. 5, X-energy selected Fluor to provide engineering, design development, supply chain, estimating, and project controls services for the nuclear island of Energy Northwest’s proposed Cascade Advanced Energy Facility near Richland, Washington, following an earlier 2026 award for similar services at Seadrift. At Cascade, Cascade Nuclear Partners, a joint venture of Kiewit, Black & Veatch, and Aecon, holds the progressive design-build contract . Sell noted that Fluor is supporting the design of systems within Cascade’s nuclear island, while Cascade Nuclear Partners is advancing the conventional island design and coordinating requirements across the broader plant.
The Cascade project, which would initially employ four Xe-100 reactors with provisions for expansion to 12 modules totaling 960 MW, would be sited near Energy Northwest’s Columbia Generating Station, where X-energy originally planned its ARDP demonstration . It is the first project under X-energy’s collaboration with Amazon , which aims to support deployment of more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.
Component Testing and Manufacturing Readiness. X-energy is expanding component fabrication, machining, and testing capabilities at its 90,000-square-foot X-energy Technology Advancement Center (XTAC) in Frederick, Maryland. The company has begun testing graphite components and expects over the next couple of years to commission a helium test loop to validate the mechanical systems that operate in the helium environment. Those systems, Sell noted, fall broadly into three groups: the fuel handling system, the helium circulator system, and the control rods and their drive mechanisms.
Sell said the testing program is intended to refine manufacturing and installation procedures and validate long-term O&M assumptions before commercial deployment, though he noted that work at XTAC is not a significant input to Dow’s preliminary investment decision. “In the simplest terms, we want to have done it at the XTAC before we do it in the field,” he said.
Component Procurement. Five days before the NRC issued Long Mott’s construction permit, X-energy announced its first procurement of steam generator tubing for the Xe-100. Swedish specialty materials manufacturer Alleima will supply specialized stainless steel tubing to South Korean nuclear component manufacturer Doosan Enerbility, which will bend it into helical coils for Long Mott’s steam generators. The companies, however, did not disclose the quantity, contract value, or delivery schedule.
The procurement follows a December 2025 agreement under which X-energy, as POWER reported , reserved manufacturing capacity at Doosan for 16 sets of reactor pressure vessels, steam generator pressure vessels, and additional steel components of the main power system. According to Doosan, the reservation covers the four proposed Long Mott reactors and the potential 12-reactor Cascade development in Washington. Doosan has also committed to building a dedicated small modular reactor fabrication facility in Changwon, South Korea, which X-energy says could support production of components for approximately 20 Xe-100 reactors annually at full capacity.
Beyond steel forgings and steam generator tubing, X-energy has secured graphite manufacturing capacity and materials through Toyo Tanso and SGL Carbon.
“Regulatory approval is not on the critical path for any of our projects. It really relates more to the supply chain, which is why we are making early investments in the supply chain because that’s the best opportunity to reduce schedule on our future projects,” Sell told analysts.
Commercial-Scale Fuel Fabrication. In Oak Ridge, Tennessee, X-energy’s wholly owned fuel subsidiary TRISO-X completed vertical construction of the shell of its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility on schedule in the third quarter of 2026, according to X-energy’s third-quarter financial results . The next phase encompasses interior buildout, installation of fuel fabrication equipment, and construction of supporting facilities, including a graphite matrix powder facility that will prepare and blend graphite materials for fuel pebble fabrication.
In February, the NRC granted TRISO-X a 40-year special nuclear material license —the first Category II fuel fabrication license for processing high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU). The DOE characterizes TX-1 as the first commercial-scale HALEU fuel fabrication facility in the U.S. to receive NRC approval.
TX-1 has a designed production capacity of approximately 700,000 fuel pebbles annually, equivalent to 5 metric tons of uranium and sufficient to support operation of up to 11 Xe-100 reactors. TRISO-X, which will also require a reliable supply of enriched uranium feedstock, received an initial HALEU allocation from the DOE in April 2025 that X-energy says will be used to manufacture fuel for Long Mott’s first core loads.
X-energy is also advancing design work for TX-2, its second planned commercial fuel fabrication facility, and TX-L, a dedicated R&D center. Costs associated with TX-2’s design and site preparation are currently being expensed rather than capitalized, Gross noted, owing to the project’s stage of development.
The company’s ambitions for TRISO-X, notably, extend beyond supplying its own reactor fleet. Sell said the Part 70 license authorizes commercial fuel manufacturing using uranium enriched up to 20% at its first two commercial facilities, and the company intends to pursue third-party customers developing reactors and microreactors that use coated particle fuel.
X-energy, meanwhile, continues to pursue qualification of its own TRISO fuel through an irradiation campaign at the Advanced Test Reactor in Idaho. Asked about the campaign on Nov. 12, Sell said interim results had met the company’s expectations, though X-energy has yet to complete the campaign and publish its assessment.
Building a Commercial Reactor Portfolio. X-energy, which reported $1.8 billion in cash and investments and no debt as of Sept. 30, has a prospective commercial portfolio encompassing 144 reactors representing approximately 11.5 GW of generating capacity, assuming each customer exercises its contingent rights in full. Of those, Sell said, up to 40 reactors are associated with identified project plans and development partnerships involving Dow, Energy Northwest, American Electric Power (AEP), and Centrica.
Beyond Long Mott and Cascade, the prospective deployments include a 960-MW project involving Amazon and AEP in Sullivan County, Indiana, where AEP is evaluating redevelopment of a former coal-fired generation site with an existing PJM Interconnection grid connection. The parties are committing resources to site characterization, feasibility studies, community engagement, preparation for a construction permit application, and development of the prospective commercial arrangement between Amazon and AEP.
In the UK, where X-energy’s Xe-100 entered the Generic Design Assessment process in September, the company is pursuing a collaboration with Centrica targeting up to 6 GW. Sell said expanded cooperation between U.S. and UK nuclear regulators enables X-energy to draw on NRC-approved technical documentation and safety analyses during the British assessment.
For X-energy, whose commercial strategy includes sales of reactor technology, associated services, and fuel over the operating lives of its customers’ plants, executing the first commercial deployment at Seadrift will be critical to establishing the cost and schedule assumptions for subsequent projects.
“This is the process. This is where we develop the mastery through repetition, to move from the first, more expensive plants all the way down to lower cost lower risk, shorter scheduled plants that can be financed and deployed at scale,” Sell said.

Lucid Gravity Robotaxis Began Public Tests in the SF Bay Area, Can It One-Up Tesla Robotaxi?
7 photos
Photo: Nuro
In July 2025, Lucid Motors, Nuro, and Uber signed a deal to launch a robotaxi service. Now, the three partners announced the beginning of driverless tests on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area. The move follows months of supervised autonomous tests, with employee driverless rides planned to start soon.
Many, and especially Tesla fans, believed that Elon Musk's company would be the only one capable of cracking autonomous driving. Even though its efforts date back more than a decade, without many achievements, they still thought others were years behind. As a Level-2 driver-assist system, the Tesla FSD (TAD in Europe) is indeed very capable. However, an autonomous driving system it is not, which Tesla makes sure you understand when you want to use it.
In the meantime, other carmakers have announced their own autonomous driving programs. This contradicted Tesla fans, who dreamed that all other carmakers would either license Tesla FSD or go extinct. Rivian is about to launch its point-to-point autonomous driving system later this year. Even Lucid Motors, a severely cash-strapped EV startup, is hoping to give Tesla a run for its money in autonomous driving.
Lucid Motors announced last year a partnership with Uber and Nuro to start driverless operations. Under the terms of this partnership, Lucid would provide the vehicles, Nuro would install the autonomous driving hardware and software, and Uber would operate the robotaxis. It was a surprising deal, considering Lucid Motors' difficulties, but one that could ensure its survival, thanks to the significant number of vehicles involved.
Now, the three partners announced that they have concluded supervised autonomous driving tests and are ready to move to the next level. That is, Lucid, Nuro, and Uber have started testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis without a driver behind the wheel in the San Francisco Bay Area. Employee rides will follow shortly, with a public launch expected in the first quarter of 2027.
Photo: Lucid Motors Previous tests with a safety driver have been conducted in the SF Bay Area and in Houston since December 2025. These tests have paved the way for driverless trials, which are now beginning in Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale. Additional Bay Area cities will follow next year. A fleet of over 100 Lucid Gravity vehicles is involved, all equipped with Nuro's autonomous driving hardware and software.
Nuro has been mostly responsible for the tests, including safety procedures and assessments, after it received two key California permits. The CPUC Drivered Pilot Permit allows for passenger rides with a safety operator. At the same time, the California DMV Driverless Testing Permit allows Nuro to start public road testing with no driver behind the wheel. Only six companies have received the latter, and Tesla is not one of them, sadly.
Uber has committed to purchasing at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with the Nuro Driver, with plans to expand across dozens of global markets. Lucid Motors is not the only carmaker that signed such a partnership with Uber. In March, Rivian also announced a $1.25 billion deal comprising up to 50,000 R2 vehicles. It's obvious that Uber is hedging its autonomous driving bets across multiple carmakers, with Hyundai also among its partners .

Two of the most interesting new electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.
Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just launched its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim. Meanwhile, ALSO, the high-tech electric bicycle startup spun out of Rivian, announced that it was halting deliveries of its futuristic TM-B electric bicycle amid mounting software problems.
Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical. Both have deep engineering roots and were incubated by successful technology companies. And both have developed impressive proprietary systems that set their bikes apart from the competition.
But their dramatically different launches offer an interesting lesson about the difference between innovation and execution, and which has proven to be more successful in the real world.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Amflow’s new UE line of commuter e-bikes was launched last week
Amflow: Making the bicycle better
Amflow’s story actually begins before the brand launched its first electric mountain bike.
DJI, the Chinese drone giant, had spent years perfecting the art of building small, lightweight, powerful electric motors, sophisticated electronic controllers, and advanced battery management systems. Those are all technologies that translate remarkably well to electric bicycles, even if the applications are quite different.
That expertise helped give rise to the Avinox e-bike drive system, which quickly earned a reputation as one of the most impressive electric bicycle drivetrains on the market. The mid-drive motor and control system rapidly ate away at the huge market share long held by Bosch and other leaders.
The motors offered an almost ridiculous amount of power in a lightweight package, paired with sophisticated sensors and software that delivered smooth, natural-feeling pedal assistance. The system was also designed as a tightly integrated ecosystem, with displays, controllers, batteries, and motors working together.
Amflow’s first electric mountain bikes demonstrated just how well that technology could work in the real world.
And now, with the launch of the new Amflow UE commuter series, the company is taking that proven technology and applying it to an entirely different kind of riding.
Amflow’s new UE commuter series applies the brand’s mountain bike expertise to a city-focused ride
The new bikes bring Avinox’s powerful pedal assistance and intelligent electronic controls to a more practical urban platform, adding commuter-focused features designed to make everyday riding more convenient.
There’s plenty of proprietary technology here, but perhaps the most important thing about Amflow’s approach is what the company didn’t reinvent.
The bikes still fundamentally work like bicycles.
You pedal, a conventional mechanical drivetrain transfers that power to the rear wheel, and an electric motor provides assistance. It’s the same basic arrangement that has worked on electric bicycles for decades, just refined with much more advanced engineering.
Amflow didn’t need to fundamentally change the bicycle to make it feel futuristic. Instead, the company focused on making the familiar bicycle experience better.
And while the new commuter models are still too fresh to judge their long-term reliability, early impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. That’s an encouraging start, especially considering the company’s already established reputation in the demanding electric mountain bike market.
ALSO’s TM-B electric bicycle is perhaps the most innovative e-bike we’ve seen launched this year
ALSO: Reinventing the bicycle itself
ALSO, on the other hand, took a dramatically different approach.
The company emerged from Rivian , the American electric vehicle manufacturer known for its technologically advanced electric trucks and SUVs.
Like DJI, Rivian has extensive experience developing sophisticated electric drivetrains, battery systems, power electronics, and software. And like Amflow, ALSO wanted to bring that expertise to a new generation of electric bicycles.
But instead of using those technologies to improve a conventional bicycle, ALSO decided to rethink the entire machine.
The company’s TM-B electric bicycle uses a pedal-by-wire system, meaning the pedals aren’t mechanically connected to the rear wheel. Instead, pedaling turns a generator that sends data signals and power through an electronic system, while software determines how the rear motor responds.
ALSO’s pedal-by-wire system is a fascinating marvel of engineering
Pedal-by-wire systems have some genuine potential advantages. They can eliminate traditional chains, belts, derailleurs, and other mechanical drivetrain components, which has helped land them on many unconventional e-bikes such as extremely long cargo e-bikes and truck-like electric bicycles that would otherwise require ridiculously long chain runs.
They can also allow engineers to completely customize the relationship between pedaling effort and motor response, creating riding experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a conventional bicycle drivetrain.
But there’s a catch. When you replace a relatively simple mechanical system with a sophisticated electronic one, you’re also introducing a lot more opportunities for things to go wrong.
And unlike a conventional bicycle, where many drivetrain problems can be diagnosed and repaired with basic tools, a highly proprietary software-defined bicycle can become much more dependent on its manufacturer to keep it running.
That’s not inherently a bad tradeoff. Modern electric cars have demonstrated that software-defined vehicles can offer tremendous benefits. But it puts enormous pressure on the manufacturer to get the hardware, software, and integration right.
Unfortunately, ALSO’s early rollout suggests that the company hasn’t quite managed that yet.
Two very different launches
The contrast between the two companies became particularly striking last week.
Amflow unveiled its new commuter models, building on the reputation of its successful electric mountain bikes and earning enthusiastic early reviews.
ALSO, meanwhile, confirmed that it was pausing deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycle due to software-related issues. That’s on top of earlier delivery delays and reports of customers having to send their new ALSO TM-B bicycles back for repairs.
We’ve also previously reported on some unusual charging and discharging behavior with the TM-B, raising questions about how the bike’s sophisticated electronic systems were managing energy. Those concerns now look particularly relevant in light of the company’s latest announcement.
To be fair, we don’t know how widespread the problems are across ALSO’s delivered bicycles, and it’s entirely possible that the company will resolve these issues relatively quickly with updates on delivered bikes and reflashing software on bikes yet to be shipped.
Nor should we assume that Amflow’s new commuter bikes will be trouble-free simply because their initial reviews are positive. Long-term reliability is something that can only be established over time. But the difference in their respective launches is hard to ignore.
Both are examples of tech-focused startups attempting to reinvent the future of e-bikes. One company is expanding its lineup after successfully establishing its technology in the market. The other is struggling to get its first product consistently into customers’ hands.
And that brings us to what I think is the most interesting part of this story.
Innovation is only half the battle
There’s a fundamental difference between developing impressive technology and successfully turning that technology into a dependable consumer product.
Both Amflow and ALSO have accomplished the first part.
The engineering behind the Avinox drive system is genuinely impressive, and the TM-B’s pedal-by-wire architecture is one of the more ambitious attempts to rethink the electric bicycle in recent years.
But Amflow appears to have taken a more measured approach to bringing that technology to consumers.
The company first developed and refined a sophisticated electric bicycle drivetrain, proved it in the demanding electric mountain bike market, and then adapted it to commuter applications.
ALSO attempted something much more ambitious right out of the gate: launching an entirely new bicycle architecture with numerous interdependent proprietary systems.
Neither approach is inherently wrong. In fact, if nobody ever attempted the latter, we’d probably miss out on some genuinely revolutionary products. But there’s a reason that so many successful technological innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary.
Two very different takes on physical design
Sometimes the smartest engineering decision isn’t figuring out how to replace something that already works. It’s figuring out how to make it work better.
And there’s a certain irony in the fact that Amflow’s new commuter bike looks relatively ordinary, yet appears to deliver an extraordinary riding experience.
ALSO’s TM-B, meanwhile, looks like something from the future, but its early ownership experience has been considerably less impressive.
Electrek’s Take
I want to be clear that I’m not rooting for or against either company here.
Quite the opposite. Both ALSO and Amflow are working to accelerate the state of the industry. I’ve been fascinated by the TM-B since it was first unveiled, and I genuinely hope the company succeeds. And Amflow has taken the fresh perspective brought by its parent company, DJI, and turned it into real-world progress. The e-bike industry needs more innovation to help push everyone forward.
I love seeing companies take big swings in the electric bicycle industry, especially when they’re attempting something more interesting than slapping a bigger motor and battery onto an otherwise generic frame.
And I think pedal-by-wire technology has real potential. The ability to electronically control the relationship between pedaling and propulsion opens up fascinating possibilities, even if it also introduces new challenges.
I should also mention that I have not personally ridden either of these bikes, and thus this is analysis from the sidelines. The Amflow UE Carbon was only unveiled a few days ago, though I’ve got one on the way and am excited to begin testing it soon and to report back here on the experience. As for ALSO, the bike was unveiled a year ago, and I was slated to be at the launch for test riding, but barely an hour after I posted an exclusive article revealing that ALSO had accidentally leaked its own images of its yet-to-be-unveiled bike on its website, I received an email uninviting me to the upcoming event and test ride.
So keep in mind that all of this is being said as an analyst with nearly two decades in the e-bike industry and hundreds of different e-bikes under my belt, not from personal experience with either bike model.
But as someone who spends an enormous amount of time riding, testing, and working on electric bicycles, I also appreciate the value of simplicity. A bicycle is an inherently elegant machine. It’s lightweight, efficient, relatively easy to maintain, and remarkably dependable considering how few components it needs to function.
Electric assistance has already made that machine dramatically more useful for millions of people. The question is how much more complexity we should introduce in pursuit of further improvements.
Amflow seems to be asking, “How can we use advanced technology to make riding a bicycle better?”
ALSO seems to be asking, “What if we could completely rethink how a bicycle works?”
Both are worthwhile questions, and I’m glad there are companies pursuing both answers. But right now, Amflow is demonstrating the advantages of building on a proven foundation, while ALSO is learning some painful lessons about the challenges of reinventing the wheel.
And perhaps that’s the biggest takeaway from this tale of two high-tech e-bike startups.
The future of electric bicycles will undoubtedly involve more sophisticated motors, batteries, sensors, and software. But the companies that succeed won’t necessarily be the ones that pack the most technology into their bikes.
They’ll be the ones that figure out how to make all that technology work so seamlessly that riders barely have to think about it.
Because at the end of the day, the best electric bicycle isn’t necessarily the one with the most advanced technology. It’s the one that makes you want to ride it every day – and actually lets you.

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce speaks Tuesday at the Ontario Critical Minerals Forum in Toronto. Credit: Blair McBride
Posted By: Blair McBride November 24, 2026
Ontario plans to overhaul mining approvals beyond its fast-track program for four major projects, proposing to eliminate or streamline half of the key permits and authorizations required to develop mines.
Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said Tuesday the government would introduce legislation next week to accelerate exploration and approvals for new and expanding mines, while introducing tougher enforcement measures and new rules aimed at preventing companies from indefinitely holding idle mining leases.
“One of the greatest concerns we heard is while One Project, One Process is a sound supercharging mechanism, how about for everyone else? For the 98% of projects not captured by the 1P1P,” Lecce told the Ontario Critical Minerals Forum in Toronto.
The proposed reforms come as Ottawa and provincial governments prioritize domestic mineral production to strengthen Canada’s economic security, reduce dependence on Chinese-controlled supply chains and respond to United States tariffs.
Cutting timelines
The government estimates the changes could save a combined 31,000 to 47,000 calendar days a year across mining permit applications.
The changes would cover new and expanding mines, as well as early and advanced exploration. Companies would be able to obtain a single exploration permit instead of several, while the validity of early exploration plans would be extended to three years from two.
“Our permits right now still take too long to get approved through government,” Lecce told reporters after his speech. “It’s a maze of bureaucracy, and it’s paralyzing investment.”
The reforms build on Ontario’s One Project, One Process framework, launched in October 2025 to halve government review times for major mining developments. Four projects have been designated so far: Frontier Lithium’s (TSXV: FL; US-OTC: LITOF) PAK lithium project, Kinross Gold’s (TSX: K; NYSE: KGC) Great Bear gold project, Canada Nickel’s (TSXV: CNC; US-OTC: CNIKF) Crawford nickel project and Mayfair Gold’s (TSXV: MFG; NYSE-A: MINE) Fenn-Gib gold project.
Mining lease changes
Lecce also announced a “Use It or Lose It” policy intended to prevent companies from indefinitely holding mining leases without advancing exploration or development. Only 15% of Ontario’s land with high mineral potential is currently available for new staking, he said.
“Some of these leases are being held for a good reason,” Lecce said, acknowledging that mining projects can take years to advance. “But others are sitting, waiting for the company that actually wants to build to come along, pay them, and get out of the way.”
Under the proposed changes, idle leases would not be renewed, allowing other companies to stake the land. Lecce said fewer than half of Ontario’s mining leases have exploration plans or permits. Lecce didn’t specify how idle leases would be defined or whether exemptions would apply to projects facing lengthy development timelines.
Enforcement changes
Lecce also outlined a graduated enforcement system that would give regulators more options for dealing with violations, including field orders, tickets and administrative monetary penalties.
The legislation would also consolidate oversight of mine tailings storage facilities under the Ministry of Energy and Mines to reduce overlap among provincial ministries, Lecce said.
Price support
Despite the government’s emphasis on countering China’s dominance of critical mineral supply chains, Lecce stopped short of committing Ontario to minimum-price guarantees that could help new mining projects secure financing.
Asked by The Northern Miner whether the province would guarantee critical mineral prices, Lecce pointed instead to Ottawa’s work with G7 partners on a critical minerals buyers’ club through the existing Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance. The alliance aims to strengthen supply chains among allied countries and reduce exposure to market concentration and manipulation.
“We’re working closely with Minister Hodgson as he works to establish a global buying club to ensure that our minerals are able to be exported to allied supply chains, and that we’re able to create price stability,” Lecce said, referring to federal Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson.
Efficiency over funding
Asked whether the new legislation would include additional funding commitments, Lecce said the government’s priority was reducing regulatory delays rather than announcing a new financing program.
“The problem we hear from industry is not a lack of capital from government or otherwise,” he said. “It’s that it takes too long to open mines because the permits get stuck in the bureaucracy.”
Lecce cited provincial support for Generation Mining’s (TSX: GENM; US-OTC: GENMF) Marathon copper-palladium project. Further investments under Ontario’s existing $500-million Critical Minerals Processing Fund will be announced in the coming weeks and months, he added.
Ontario announced up to $11 million in conditional loan support for Marathon’s processing facility in September . Lecce didn’t identify which additional projects might receive support in 2027.
Separately, Lecce said Ontario plans to release a new minerals strategy in March 2027, ahead of the Prospectors & Developers Association of Canada convention in Toronto. The document will expand the province’s existing focus on critical minerals to include gold, industrial minerals and the broader mining sector, he said.

Reggie Jackson's Ferrari 250 GT Lusso Failed To Clear Reserve After High Bid Hit $1.1 Million
14 photos
Photo: P1Miami on Bring a Trailer
Someone put $1,103,019 on the table for a 1963 Ferrari 250 GT Lusso. Not any ol' GTL, but chassis number 250GTL5117, namely the car owned by Reggie Jackson between 1998 and 2008. Alas, the Bring a Trailer auction closed with the reserve unmet, and it's easy to understand why.
Every single GTL auctioned thus far in 2026 fetched over a mil, with chassis number 5593 changing hands for $3.3 million at Mecum Kissimmee in January. Given this information, the seller was perfectly in the right not to be pleased with merely $1.1 million for the ex-Reggie Jackson car.
Ferrari produced just around 350 examples between 1962 and 1964, and the Scaglietti-bodied Lusso is definitely a looker. One of the prettiest Fezzas of all time also marked the end of the 250 series. It and the race-oriented GTO were replaced by the punchier 275 and 330 lines for 1964.
This particular vehicle comes with Ferrari Classiche certification and an extensive ownership file. Still, it's not a perfect 250 GT Lusso. This one has changed paint colors, received a substantial refurbishment, accumulated some paint damage, and carries a replacement limited-slip differential instead of the original unit.
The 125th 250 GT Lusso built was completed on October 19, 1963, then subsequently delivered to a Rome-based dealer. A construction company acquired it before selling the car to a Swiss gentleman in May 1964. Six years later, Luigi Chinetti Motors brought the car to the United States of America.
Photo: P1Miami on Bring a Trailer Its Rhode Island-based owner from that era kept the V12-powered grand tourer for a quarter of a century. Baseball Hall of Famer Reggie Jackson entered the scene in 1998, commissioning Grand Prix Motors in California to refurbish the car two years later.
Work included a paint job, switching from the original Marrone to Pino Verde. Tobacco leather upholstery also needs mentioning, another unoriginal element that affects 250GTL5117's value.
Jackson ultimately sold the Ferrari in 2008 to a Midwest collector, who entrusted further work to Greg Jones. The following year, chassis number 5117 collected a Platinum Award at the Cavallino Classic in Florida. Classiche certification followed in 2011, while the current owner got their hands on it back in 2018.
Pictured with cracked paint aft of the passenger door, 5117 rolls on Michelin XVS rubber mounted on 15-inch Borrani wire wheels. A matching spare sits in the trunk. Under the hood, you will find a 3.0-liter naturally aspirated V12 and three Weber carbs. All three were rebuilt in 2026, while the engine received a valve job during the Greg Jones refurbishment from two decades ago.
The oil, spark plugs, and fuel filter were changed in 2026 as well, yet the listing mentions a bit of seepage on certain mechanical components. Prior to the Bring a Trailer auction, the odometer showed 30,359 original kilometers (18,864 miles). The seller added just around 50 clicks (31 miles).
Offered with a Marcel Massini report, historical invoices, an owner's manual, previous ownership photos, and a tool kit, the Montana-titled car has plenty going for it. The bidding result, however, is a reminder that provenance and a seven-figure reserve don't always find common ground.

View of the Marimaca property in Chile. Credit: Marimaca Copper.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 24, 2026
Developer Marimaca Copper (TSX: MARI; ASX: MC2) has secured investment committee backing from a Sprott (TSX, NYSE: SII) unit for a proposed funding package to help build its main copper project in northern Chile.
Vancouver-based Marimaca signed a non-binding term sheet with Sprott Resource Lending for up to $450 million (C$646.6 million), including $425 million in senior secured debt, according to a statement Tuesday . Sprott will also make an equity investment of up to $25 million.
The first $100 million of the loan would become available after a construction decision, subject to final agreements and other conditions. Sprott must still complete financial and legal due diligence.
Marimaca is heading into 2027 “with detailed engineering, site activity and construction preparation set to accelerate” at the oxide project in the coming months, President Nico Cookson said.
13-year mine
The Marimaca oxide project, about 45 km from Antofagasta, would cost $587 million to build and produce an average of 43,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year over 13 years, according to Marimaca’s 2025 feasibility study.
Marimaca had $127 million in cash and equivalents at Sept. 30. It still has to arrange the rest of the construction financing.
The planned open-pit operation would use heap leaching to recover copper. Its location near highways, power lines and the port of Mejillones provides access to existing infrastructure. Marimaca received environmental approval in November 2025 and is pursuing the remaining construction permits.
In a report issued last week, National Bank Financial analyst Andrew Dusome pointed to a targeted final investment decision in mid-2027. He also expected Pampa Medina’s first resource estimate in the first half of next year.
Upside potential
The 7½-year loan would carry a minimum interest rate of 8.5%. Sprott would charge 5.75 percentage points over the secured overnight financing rate, a United States benchmark, with a floor of 2.75% on the benchmark. Principal repayments would begin on March 31, 2031. The lender would require neither copper-price hedges nor payments tied to production.
The terms would allow Marimaca to keep drilling its nearby Pampa Medina copper-silver discovery during construction. Drill hole SPRD-21 cut 102 metres at 1% copper and 5.1 grams silver per tonne from 706 metres downhole, the company reported Nov. 19.
Ongoing drilling at Pampa Medina “continues to expand the mineralized area of interest with large step-out holes and prove out the high-grade central zone,” Dusome wrote. He highlighted the project’s “strong upside potential.”
Mine financier
Sprott Resource Lending, a wholly owned subsidiary of asset manager Sprott, arranges debt financing for mining companies.
In August, Wia Gold (ASX: WIA) agreed non-binding terms with the lender for $360 million in debt and a $15 million equity subscription to help develop Namibia’s Kokoseb gold project. Emerald Resources (ASX: EMR) also signed a mandate with Sprott and Macquarie Bank for a proposed $200 million acquisition facility during the September quarter.
Marimaca shares dropped 1.8% to C$5.86 Tuesday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$794 million ($555 million). The stock has traded between C$5.53 and C$13.49 in the past year.

EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
Stellantis North America Patents New-Gen Jeep Compass in the US
19 photos
Photo: USPTO/FCA
Stellantis has recently secured US-market design protection for a Jeep model that American customers still cannot purchase. D1,157,295 S is the design patent for the new-gen Compass, which is codenamed J4U in Euro-market specification. Built in Italy at the Melfi plant on STLA Medium underpinnings from the Peugeot 3008 and Opel Grandland, this SUV may not even be sold in North America.
The United States Patent and Trademark Office granted the design patent to FCA US LLC earlier this month, following an application from February 2025. All drawings show the exterior from a bunch of angles. The squarer body of the J4U is joined by more pronounced wheel arches, pretty slim lighting elements, and a reinterpreted seven-slot grille that doesn't look Jeep enough if you ask me.
Meanwhile, American dealer lots still get the second-generation Compass. Identified as MP, this fellow entered model year 2027 with little in the way of changes from 2026. Prices kick off at $29,900 as of this writing, and prospective customers are offered five choices. All come with 2.0-liter turbo inline-four muscle and all-wheel drive, albeit not every AWD system is created equal.
Active Drive is the lesser of two all-wheel-drive systems. Standard on four grades, Active Drive features a disconnecting power transfer unit, 4WD Lock mode, and on-demand operation. Most of the time, the American Compass is front-wheel drive to maximize fuel economy. Exclusive to the Trailhawk, the Active Drive Low system rocks a two-speed PTU and a shorter final drive ratio.
Engaging 4WD Low in the Trailhawk locks the front and rear axles together, and 20:1 is the advertised crawl ratio. Rock mode and Hill Descent Control are other highlights that make this grade stand out in the crowd. Regardless of grade, the Compass for North America packs 200 horsepower and an eight-speed auto.
Photo: Jeep The J4U for Europe is longer than its predecessor, and its 110-inch (2,795 millimeters) wheelbase provides quite a bit more room between the axles. Powertrain options kick off with a mild-hybrid I3 turbo, followed by a 1.6-liter turbo inline-four with plug-in hybrid assistance. Full-electric options are available as well, including a 4xe-branded EV with two electric drive units. The 4xe develops 375 ps (370 hp) and 577 Nm (426 lb-ft) of combined torque.
Having cleared all that up, why isn't the European Compass being adapted for North America? The answer comes from none other than Stellantis North America, which confirmed in August 2026 that Belvidere Assembly is gearing up for STLA One production. The next-generation Cherokee is listed as the first vehicle on that platform, with pilot production kicking off in 2028.
Belvidere will assemble a minimum of two vehicles on the STLA One, and the second one should be the Compass for North America. The Auburn Hills-based automaker has committed $800 million for said plant. Unfortunately, both the all-new Cherokee and Compass for America are to start production in 2029.
STLA One is likely to merge and phase out a bunch of platforms. STLA Large and STLA Frame are understood to remain untouched as the other two pillars in the automaker's strategy to put 50 percent of global volume onto three core vehicle architectures by 2030.

Rail volume hit a new five-year high and the spot-to-contract spread narrowed to its closest level to breakeven since the beginning of October. Rejections jumped 91 basis points to their highest reading since late October. The three-month outlook slips a point to 76.
This week’s SONAR Pricing Power Index (PPI): 73 (up from 68).
The composite rose five points, with broad gains across capacity and pricing. The rejection rate jumped 91 basis points to 13.68%, moving to the 83rd percentile from the 77th. Van rejections surged to 11.35% from 10.11%. Rail volume hit a new five-year high at 36,665 loaded containers, reaching the 100th percentile from the 99th. The national spot rate rose to $3.61 a mile, moving to the 98th percentile from the 97th, and the spot-to-contract spread narrowed to negative $0.11 in the weekly series from negative $0.23, moving to the 81st percentile from the 76th. Intermodal contract rates moved to the 71st percentile from the 65th. Partly offsetting those gains, accepted truckload volume rose about 2% to 9,810 but remained in the 21st percentile, ocean bookings were essentially flat at 1,856 in the 44th percentile, and van contract rates eased slightly to the 89th percentile from the 90th.

source_document.body:
The first fully electric Porsche Boxster is finally in the home stretch of development. Ahead of its official debut in early 2027, Porsche offered an early look at the two-door electric sports car.
Porsche confirms the electric Boxster will debut in 2027
Despite rumors that the all-electric 718 Boxster was canceled, Porsche confirmed on Tuesday that the Boxster EV will debut in the first quarter of 2027.
“Starting next year, the all-electric 718 Boxster will offer our customers a compelling entry point into the world of two-door sports cars,” Porsche CEO Dr Michael Leiters said.
Ahead of its upcoming debut, Porsche is putting the electric sports car through the paces to ensure it preserves the DNA of its predecessors, a top priority.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Porsche developed a new “E-Core” architecture specifically for the 718 Boxster to lower the seat position and optimize weight distribution.
With the 800-volt battery mounted directly behind the seats, where the internal combustion engine would typically be found, the weight is concentrated toward the middle of the vehicle. The electric Boxster has a weight distribution of 40% on the front axle and 60% on the rear, matching that of a traditional mid-engined sports car.
Porsche electric 718 Boxster prototype (Source: Porsche)
It also features an “intelligent lightweight construction,” as Porsche calls it, so the vehicle’s overall weight matches that of the current 911 Cabriolet models with its T-Hybrid powertrain.
“Our engineers have succeeded in transferring the Boxster’s unique concept to the electric world, further enhancing it in the process,” Porsche’s CEO said.
The electric Boxster shares many chassis components with the 911, including the steering, which is based on the 911 Carrera GTS. It will offer rear-axle steering, a first for the 718 Boxster.
Porsche electric 718 Boxster prototype (Source: Porsche)
Meanwhile, the wheel and tire dimensions and braking system are based on the Porsche 911, and the electronically controlled PTV+ limited-slip differential is also pulled from the 911.
Porsche said the electric Boxster will be “the most powerful 718 ever,” but didn’t offer a specific output figure.
The range-topping Boxster EV can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under three seconds, according to Porsche, and it can reach a top speed of over 155 mph (250 km/h).
All electric Boxster models will be RWD and come standard with E-Shift. Like Hyundai’s performance N EVs, including the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, the Porsche Boxster EV features a virtual gear shift that simulates the feeling and sounds of a seven-speed PDK transmission.
When E-Shift mode is not active, the paddle can be used to toggle between three levels of recuperation.
The electric Porsche 718 Boxster will make its official debut in the first quarter of 2027, so we should learn more details soon. IT will be built at Porsche’s main plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen, Germany.
